messages.subject: IRT/Differential Item Functioning
parts:
Hello,
I am fitting an IRT model with different parameters across three groups. There are four items -- the first item has the same thresholds and discrimination parameters across the three groups. Items 2,3, and 4 items have different discrimination and difficulty parameters across the three groups. My model seems to produce reasonable estimates after about 10,000 iterations, but I get the following warning messages.

Exception thrown at line 61: ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -132.734, but must be greater     1
Exception thrown at line 61: ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -133.357, but must be greater     1
Exception thrown at line 61: ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -16039.1, but must be greater     1
Exception thrown at line 61: ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -193.489, but must be greater     1
Exception thrown at line 61: ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -32.2608, but must be greater     1
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

After glancing at posts regarding similar questions, I'm under the impression this probably isn't terribly disconcerting and relatively common for a model with ordered cutpoints.

I'm more concerned about the following warning :

1: There were 1254 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help. 
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
  
I've adjusted both adapt_delta (increased to 0.95) and I increased  max_treedepth = 12.However, I still get the same warning. I've also used pairs(), to search for sampling problems -- the problem is there are so many parameters that I've been unable to pinpoint the problem. Does anyone have any thoughts on this? 

Thanks in advance,
Chris

If everything's sampling properly, there should be zero
divergent transitions after warmup. Any more than zero is
cause for concern.

The warning got cut off in the message.

But these are inconsistent in the model. Every variable
needs to have support on values that satisfy its constraints.

The tau are declared unconstrained other than relative to each other:

> ordered[C-1] tau_g1[K-1]; //Number of freed parameters, minus one for the anchor
> ordered[C-1] tau_g2[K-1];
> ordered[C-1] tau_g3[K-1];
> ordered[C-1] tau;
then their support it is only (-10, 10).

> tau_g1[k] ~ uniform(-10, 10);
> tau_g2[k] ~ uniform(-10, 10);
> tau_g3[k] ~ uniform(-10, 10);
>
> }
> tau ~ uniform(-10, 10);

We don't recommend these hard constraints anyway on statistical
grounds. So you can instead change this to a softer constraint
like:

tau ~ normal(0, 5);

- Bob

I dug into the error message. Is that really getting cut off
and showing up as "greater 1"? If so, we need to fix the
message or formatting.

The problem you're running into is that the cutpoints are
piling up on top of each other, but our error message isn't clear
enough to indicate that.

The root cause is the usual separability issue. With no prior that
keeps the cut points away from each other, they can pile up
if there are no outcomes in a band. What you need is something
like a prior on their differences rather than independent priors.
We've been thinking about this, but I don't think anyone has any
conclusive recommendations.

You can put priors on the diffs using

tail(c, K-1) - head(c, K - 1) ~ some zero-avoiding, positive constrained prior

But then I think you need a way to keep them anchored so they
don't drift, like say

c[0] ~ normal(0, 10)

or something.

- Bob

P.S. You can do exactly the same thing in Stan as in JAGS/BUGS, though it
looks like

to_vector(kappa0) ~ normal(0, 10);

kappa[j] <- sort(kappa0);

But you're much much better off just declaring kappa as ordered in Stan.
You get odd index swapping with things like the sort that are hard to deal
with in the posterior.

[changing subject to get Andrew's attention]

For those just joining us, the topic is how to put a prior on
parameters declared as:

ordered[K] c;

in an ordinal logistic regression to avoid having two cutpoints
collapse on top of each other (in traditional separability form).

I think it's enough to put a zero-avoiding, positive-constrained
prior on the differences, as in:

for (k in 2:K)
(c[k] - c[k - 1]) ~ gamma(2, 2);

I don't have a good recommendation for the parametric form of prior,
so gamma(2, 2) is pulled out of thin air. You could also use
a lognormal.

The transform's linear, so you don't need a Jacobian correction.

- Bob

Ben and I have discussed this; indeed we were planning to write a short paper on this a couple years ago. For full Bayes, a uniform prior on the constrained parameters should be fine. For posterior mode estimation, you would want a prior that is boundary-avoiding. Here we’d recommend setting up the prior as pseudo-data, some fraction of a data point within each cell.

parts:
The problem is that there's no data in some of the bins,
so they collapse on each other. Sort of like separability
in a lgoistic regression. I think Ben had suggested in the past
that we use something like a Dirichlet prior with a prior pseudocount
in each bin, and then take a cumulative sum for cutpoints:

parameters {
simplex[K] c_raw;
...

transformed parameters {
ordered[K] c;
c <- cumulative_sum(theta_raw);

model {
c_raw ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(2, K));

This puts a pseudo-count of 1 in each bin in the prior and
scales the cutpoints in (0, 1). You could translate and
scale the cumulative sum to get a different range.

Should the cutpoints be scaled to (0, 1) or (-0.5, 0.5)
or (-1, 1) or what? I assume the scale doesn't really matter
because it'll just determine the scale of the regression
coefficients in the ordered logistic. But there's also a pesky
intercept parameter that'll also get involved in the identifiability.

This should all go in the manual, assuming I'm thinking about
it the right way.

- Bob

parts:
With flat priors on the cutpoint parameters, the bins should not collapse onto each other. At least, I think not. Not in full Bayes. I guess I’ll have to think more about this.

> parameters {
> simplex[K] c_raw;
> ...
